How to Play Ticket to Ride in 2026: Rules and How to Win

2026-10-09

How to play Ticket to Ride, in one breath: every turn you do exactly one of three things. Draw two train cards, spend a matching set to claim a route, or draw more destination tickets. Connect the cities on your tickets, finish with the most points, and you win. It seats 2 to 5 people, runs about 45 minutes, and most groups are playing inside five minutes.

I have taught this game at least 30 times, and the rules are never the hard part. The hard part is that half the how-to pages still teach the 2004 rulebook. Days of Wonder refreshed the base game in 2025 with new art, bigger cards, and a small rules tune-up, and this walkthrough follows the copy you actually buy today.

Below is the whole game in the order it clicks. What is in the box, setup, your turn, how scoring works, the ending trigger, and one buried rule that quietly decides most two-player games.

What Is in the Box

You get a map of North America, a pile of plastic trains, and two decks of cards. Each player takes one color. There are 45 trains per color, plus a wooden scoring marker that starts on the track running around the board's edge.

Then the train car cards. Eight colors plus a wild Locomotive, 110 cards in all. These are your money. You spend them to lay track. The destination tickets are the other deck, and they are the secret half of the game. A ticket names two cities and a point value, and nobody else sees it until the end.

Setup in 90 Seconds

Give everyone a color, a scoring marker on the start space, and 4 train car cards. Shuffle the rest of that deck, deal 5 face up beside the board, and set the Longest Path Bonus card next to the map.

Then the destination tickets. In older copies you deal 3 and each player keeps at least 2. In the 2025 Refresh you deal 4 and keep at least 2, which gives everyone a slightly better first plan. Either way, tickets stay face down in front of you, secret until scoring.

Your Turn: Pick One of Three

On your turn you do one thing, and only one. Then play passes to the left.

Draw train car cards. Take 2 cards, either off the table or blind off the top of the deck. One catch: if you take a face-up Locomotive, you only draw 1 card that turn. A Locomotive pulled blind is friendlier. It still counts as a single card, and you can keep drawing your second.

Claim a route. Play a set of cards that match one route's color and length, then drop your trains on it. A 3-length blue route needs 3 blue cards. Gray routes are the flexible ones, since any single color set works on them. Locomotives are wild and fit anywhere.

Draw destination tickets. Pull 3 fresh tickets and keep at least 1. The ones you reject go to the bottom of the deck.

Here is the key insight about that list. Two of the three actions build your score, but only one puts trains on the board. Everything else is quietly feeding that single move.

What a Route Is Worth

Route length sets the payout, and the curve is steep on purpose.

Route lengthPoints
2 trains2
3 trains4
4 trains7
5 trains10
6 trains15

Pay attention to this number: a 6-train route pays 15 points, more than double a 4-train route for two extra cards. Long routes are where the raw points hide. Two 6-train routes hand you 30 points. Five short 2-train routes hand you 10, for almost the same number of trains.

Destination Tickets Are Where Games Are Won

Routes are the visible score. Tickets are the real one. A single ticket can be worth 20 points, and they decide most games.

At the end, every ticket you completed adds its value. Every ticket you kept and failed subtracts its full value. That minus sign is the entire tension of the game. A 20-point ticket you cannot finish is a 20-point hole, not a harmless miss.

This makes the mid-game ticket draw the sharpest decision on the board. Take that action, pull 3 new tickets, and you might find a cheap 12 points you can already reach. Or you add a route you will never complete and sink your own score. I watched a friend draw late, keep two big tickets, miss both, and lose a game he was winning by 15.

Here is the part nobody tells you: every point on a ticket you keep is a promise you have to pay at the end. The rulebook hands you the penalty in one quiet line and trusts you to feel the weight. Drawing tickets at the wrong moment is how good players lose.

The Rule Nobody at Your Table Knows

I thought I knew this game cold after a hundred plays. Then I read the one rulebook line I had skipped every single time, and my two-player games changed overnight.

Here is the contradiction. On the map, some pairs of cities are joined by two parallel routes. Almost everyone treats both as open. They are not. In a 2 or 3 player game, only one track of every double route can ever be used. Once someone claims it, the twin is dead for the rest of the game.

At four and five players, both tracks stay live for different people. At two and three, the map is far tighter than it looks. New players leave a double route alone because they assume the other half will still be there later. It will not.

And a second buried rule while we are here. A player may never claim both tracks of the same double route, even at five players. Pick a side and commit to it. Most tables never enforce the rule, and it sits right there in the book.

Ending the Game and Scoring

The end is triggered by running out of trains, not points. When a player finishes a turn with 0, 1, or 2 trains left in their supply, everyone gets one final turn. Then you score.

Add up the routes you claimed during the game. Reveal your tickets, add the ones you completed, and subtract the ones you did not. Give 10 points to whoever has the Longest Continuous Path of connected trains. A continuous path is one unbroken chain of your own color. Loops count, and you can pass through a city twice, but never use the same train piece two times.

The most points wins. Ties go to whoever completed more destination tickets. Still tied, the Longest Continuous Path card breaks it.

How to Actually Win

Beginners chase big routes. Better players manage tickets. A few habits separate the two.

Draw a fresh set of tickets in the middle of the game, not the end. Around turn six or seven you usually have a small network, so new tickets are cheap to slot in. Late tickets are a coin flip, because you will not have time to build the lines they ask for.

Chase the long routes early. A 6-train route is 15 points, and it eats board space the others need. Claiming it early is a double win, points plus denial.

Watch which colors are drying up. If four green cards sit face up and everyone keeps grabbing them, that green route you want is contested. Take the safe route instead of the greedy one.

And if you play with two people, remember the closed double track. A route that looks open is not, and locking a corridor early is how you win the small games.

The 2026 Refresh, and What Changed

The honest part is this. Days of Wonder refreshed the base game in 2025 and never published a clean changelist, so plenty of pages are still describing the old box. Here is what actually changed on the shelf.

New art across the board and box. Larger, easier-to-handle train and ticket cards. A cleaner rulebook. Three extra destination tickets, taking the base from 30 up to 33. And that opening deal, now 4 tickets where you keep at least 2.

The game underneath is identical. Every old expansion still works with the Refresh. If a video from 2018 taught you to play, you already know the new copy. Only the setup deal and the extra tickets are worth re-learning.

Which Box to Buy

So now you know the rules. The next question is which of the many Ticket to Ride boxes is yours.

Start with the base game, the North America map. It is the one everyone means when they say Ticket to Ride. The 2025 Refresh runs about $39.99, and it dips toward $30 when a sale hits. It is the cleanest first buy for a family or a fresh game night. My Ticket to Ride page has the stats.

If you want a meatier map, Ticket to Ride: Europe adds tunnels, ferries, and train stations that stop you from getting stuck. It runs about $40, and the extra rules add maybe three minutes to the teach. Grab it after the base game clicks, not before.

Playing with younger kids? Ticket to Ride: First Journey strips the game down to a 6-and-up version with a shorter map and simpler tickets. Same core idea, half the reading.

For veterans who want more variety, the USA 1910 expansion still works with the Refresh and adds a pile of new tickets. But the base box now ships with 33 tickets, so you can wait a while before you need it.

Where Ticket to Ride Falls Short

The card draw can decide a game before it starts. You can play every turn correctly, get starved of one color, and watch another player cruise to 80 points. It is a light game with real luck inside it, and heavy strategy players feel that fast.

The other knock is familiarity. Play it 50 times and the map stops surprising you. Routes turn into muscle memory and the tension drops. It is a gateway game first, a lifelong obsession second.

One practical limit worth knowing before you buy. The base game caps at five players. If your game night regularly pulls six or more, this box will not cover you, and you are better off splitting into two tables or picking a party game built for a crowd.

Neither flaw has stopped it from selling more than 20 million copies since 2004. The luck is the same thing that lets a first-timer beat a veteran, and that is the whole point of a game you pull out for company.

The Shelf Test

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this game survive 10 plays on a shelf that already holds 40 boxes? Ticket to Ride clears it without thinking. It is the game I reach for when the table is mixed, someone is new, and I do not want to teach for 20 minutes.

Here is the part that matters. Grab the base Ticket to Ride (Refresh) at about $40 if you want the classic everyone already knows, or Ticket to Ride: Europe at about $40 if your group already plays games and wants a bigger map. Both prices bounce, so catch the base under $35 and Europe under $38 and you have done well.
